ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Study procedures were approved by the Technical University of Munich ethics committee (786/20 S-SR).
After 90 trials, color-risk associations of low and high-risk balloons reversed; afterwards participants completed a single-color low-risk control condition.

Briefly, the BART is a computerized task where participants are presented with a series of virtual balloons and decide whether to press a button to pump the balloon, making the balloon grow larger and accumulating a small amount of money in a temporary bank, but also risking the possibility of the balloon exploding and therefore losing all temporary earnings for that trial.

Our analysis included 118 participants (mean age: 41.3, range: 18-68; 63 female, 52 male, 3 diverse) from the online platform Prolific who had an approval rating of at least 95% on Prolific and at least 20 studies completed previously.

We originally recruited 175 participants from Prolific, but 57 were excluded due to technical issues (2), withdrawn consent (3), or failed attention checks (52) which were placed within the subclinical and demographic questionnaires.

Participants completed the BART with three balloon colors of varying risk levels and a reversal of risk contingencies (bonus earnings: M=£2.97, SD=£1.01; maximum possible: £15.12) and a control version of the BART with a single fixed-contingency color association (bonus earnings: M=£3.95, SD=£1.55; maximum possible: £19.20).
If participants were inactive for more than one minute during the online session, they were removed from the study.
Prior to the BART, participants completed a guided practice (see supplementary materials Figure 1).
table.formatted: Prior to the BART, participants completed a guided practice (see supplementary materials Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

table.text: A balloon color not used in the task appeared next to written task instructions, and participants had to pump the balloon five times by pressing a keyboard button before pressing a different button to cash-in the balloon.

Participants were presented with two sets of 90 trials with three different balloon colors (Fig. 3) that corresponded to low, medium and high-risk balloons according to the different uniform distributions that breakpoints were sampled from.
table.formatted: Participants were presented with two sets of 90 trials with three different balloon colors (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>) that corresponded to low, medium and high-risk balloons according to the different uniform distributions that breakpoints were sampled from.

table.text: Participants were rewarded with bonus earnings of 0.3 pence (GBP) per pump for successfully cashed-in trials due to the large amount of trials presented, and this was determined to provide a meaningful monetary incentive according to average scores from university students testing our technical implementation of the task.

Participants were not informed of risk probabilities of the balloons or the existence of risk-level differences between colors, and they subsequently had to discover the average breakpoints through trial and error to maximize earnings.

Pre-reversal, participants were entirely naïve to balloon contingencies (e.g., blue: most rewarding), whereas the post-reversal, the most punishing balloon color became the most rewarding (i.e. orange), and the control balloon (i.e. pink) was tested in a separate set of single fixed-contingency trials.

This censoring problem has been highlighted in methodological work on the BART, as exploded trials may reveal the level of risk participants were willing to take but are omitted from the standard adjusted-pumps metric (Coon & Lee, 2022; De Groot, 2020; Young & McCoy, 2019).
table.formatted: This censoring problem has been highlighted in methodological work on the BART, as exploded trials may reveal the level of risk participants were willing to take but are omitted from the standard adjusted-pumps metric <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Coon & Lee, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">De Groot, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Young & McCoy, 2019)</ref>.

table.text: Importantly, this model performed well in the control condition, which most closely resembles a fixed-contingency task, but also in the reversal condition, where participants had to update previously learned associations.
All participants provided informed consent for participation in data collection and publication prior to the study.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> After 90 trials, color-risk associations of low and high-risk balloons reversed; afterwards participants completed a single-color low-risk control condition.

> Briefly, the BART is a computerized task where participants are presented with a series of virtual balloons and decide whether to press a button to pump the balloon, making the balloon grow larger and accumulating a small amount of money in a temporary bank, but also risking the possibility of the balloon exploding and therefore losing all temporary earnings for that trial.

> Our analysis included 118 participants (mean age: 41.3, range: 18-68; 63 female, 52 male, 3 diverse) from the online platform Prolific who had an approval rating of at least 95% on Prolific and at least 20 studies completed previously.

> We originally recruited 175 participants from Prolific, but 57 were excluded due to technical issues (2), withdrawn consent (3), or failed attention checks (52) which were placed within the subclinical and demographic questionnaires.

> Participants completed the BART with three balloon colors of varying risk levels and a reversal of risk contingencies (bonus earnings: M=£2.97, SD=£1.01; maximum possible: £15.12) and a control version of the BART with a single fixed-contingency color association (bonus earnings: M=£3.95, SD=£1.55; maximum possible: £19.20).

> If participants were inactive for more than one minute during the online session, they were removed from the study.

> Prior to the BART, participants completed a guided practice (see supplementary materials Figure 1).

> A balloon color not used in the task appeared next to written task instructions, and participants had to pump the balloon five times by pressing a keyboard button before pressing a different button to cash-in the balloon.

> Participants were presented with two sets of 90 trials with three different balloon colors (Fig. 3) that corresponded to low, medium and high-risk balloons according to the different uniform distributions that breakpoints were sampled from.

> Participants were rewarded with bonus earnings of 0.3 pence (GBP) per pump for successfully cashed-in trials due to the large amount of trials presented, and this was determined to provide a meaningful monetary incentive according to average scores from university students testing our technical implementation of the task.

> Participants were not informed of risk probabilities of the balloons or the existence of risk-level differences between colors, and they subsequently had to discover the average breakpoints through trial and error to maximize earnings.

> Pre-reversal, participants were entirely naïve to balloon contingencies (e.g., blue: most rewarding), whereas the post-reversal, the most punishing balloon color became the most rewarding (i.e. orange), and the control balloon (i.e. pink) was tested in a separate set of single fixed-contingency trials.

> This censoring problem has been highlighted in methodological work on the BART, as exploded trials may reveal the level of risk participants were willing to take but are omitted from the standard adjusted-pumps metric (Coon & Lee, 2022; De Groot, 2020; Young & McCoy, 2019).

> Importantly, this model performed well in the control condition, which most closely resembles a fixed-contingency task, but also in the reversal condition, where participants had to update previously learned associations.

> All participants provided informed consent for participation in data collection and publication prior to the study.

> Study procedures were approved by the Technical University of Munich ethics committee (786/20 S-SR).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.text: Performance relative to the maximum did not differ significantly between the reversal task (M=19.65%, SD=6.70%) and the control task (M=20.59%, SD=8.05%; paired t-test, t(117)=-1.63, p=0.105, 95% CI [-2.07, 0.20]).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.105", "p=0.137", "p=0.102"), Sentence = c("Performance relative to the maximum did not differ significantly between the reversal task (M=19.65%, SD=6.70%) and the control task (M=20.59%, SD=8.05%; paired t-test, t(117)=-1.63, p=0.105, 95% CI [-2.07, 0.20]).", "Steiger-Williams tests provided no evidence that the pre-and post-reversal traitparameter correlations differed significantly (p=0.137-0.532; Supplementary Table 10).", "However, leave-one-out analyses showed that the correlations remained significant across all participant exclusions, except for the pre-reversal correlation between risk preference and SPQ total, which became nonsignificant when the most influential participant was removed (p=0.102; Supplementary Table 9)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. We examined 346 columns across 6 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Study procedures were approved by the Technical University of Munich ethics committee (786/20 S-SR).
live_data_statements: After 90 trials, color-risk associations of low and high-risk balloons reversed; afterwards participants completed a single-color low-risk control condition.

Briefly, the BART is a computerized task where participants are presented with a series of virtual balloons and decide whether to press a button to pump the balloon, making the balloon grow larger and accumulating a small amount of money in a temporary bank, but also risking the possibility of the balloon exploding and therefore losing all temporary earnings for that trial.

Our analysis included 118 participants (mean age: 41.3, range: 18-68; 63 female, 52 male, 3 diverse) from the online platform Prolific who had an approval rating of at least 95% on Prolific and at least 20 studies completed previously.

We originally recruited 175 participants from Prolific, but 57 were excluded due to technical issues (2), withdrawn consent (3), or failed attention checks (52) which were placed within the subclinical and demographic questionnaires.

Participants completed the BART with three balloon colors of varying risk levels and a reversal of risk contingencies (bonus earnings: M=£2.97, SD=£1.01; maximum possible: £15.12) and a control version of the BART with a single fixed-contingency color association (bonus earnings: M=£3.95, SD=£1.55; maximum possible: £19.20).
If participants were inactive for more than one minute during the online session, they were removed from the study.
Prior to the BART, participants completed a guided practice (see supplementary materials Figure 1).

A balloon color not used in the task appeared next to written task instructions, and participants had to pump the balloon five times by pressing a keyboard button before pressing a different button to cash-in the balloon.

Participants were presented with two sets of 90 trials with three different balloon colors (Fig. 3) that corresponded to low, medium and high-risk balloons according to the different uniform distributions that breakpoints were sampled from.

Participants were rewarded with bonus earnings of 0.3 pence (GBP) per pump for successfully cashed-in trials due to the large amount of trials presented, and this was determined to provide a meaningful monetary incentive according to average scores from university students testing our technical implementation of the task.

Participants were not informed of risk probabilities of the balloons or the existence of risk-level differences between colors, and they subsequently had to discover the average breakpoints through trial and error to maximize earnings.

Pre-reversal, participants were entirely naïve to balloon contingencies (e.g., blue: most rewarding), whereas the post-reversal, the most punishing balloon color became the most rewarding (i.e. orange), and the control balloon (i.e. pink) was tested in a separate set of single fixed-contingency trials.

This censoring problem has been highlighted in methodological work on the BART, as exploded trials may reveal the level of risk participants were willing to take but are omitted from the standard adjusted-pumps metric (Coon & Lee, 2022; De Groot, 2020; Young & McCoy, 2019).

Importantly, this model performed well in the control condition, which most closely resembles a fixed-contingency task, but also in the reversal condition, where participants had to update previously learned associations.
All participants provided informed consent for participation in data collection and publication prior to the study.

#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 15 scripts: 8 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **3 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `ewmv_trait_robustness_verify.R` (param_q_heatmap.R); `ewmv_trait_robustness.R` (param_q_heatmap.R); `ewmv_pre_post_spearman.R` (spq_factors.R). Then these ran to the end: `ewmv_trait_robustness_verify.R`, `ewmv_trait_robustness.R`, `ewmv_pre_post_spearman.R`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **3 scripts looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/param_q_heatmap.R` to `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/analysis/plotting/param_q_heatmap.R` for `ewmv_cutdown_heatmap.R`; `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/ewmv_cutdown_heatmap.R` to `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/analysis/plotting/ewmv_cutdown_heatmap.R` for `ewmv_pre_post_spearman.R`; `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/questionnaire_meta.R` to `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/analysis/plotting/questionnaire_meta.R` for `questionnaire_figures.R`; `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/spq_factors.R` to `BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study.zip/BART_Reversal_Analysis_Online_Study-f2bedb261d3a5a7e14ed7a27e26cbb18aa7d61f0/analysis/plotting/analysis/plotting/spq_factors.R` for `ewmv_cutdown_heatmap.R`. >     draws_rds    = here::here("mcmc", "ewmv_subject_draws.rds"),
>     method = "pearson", alpha = 0.05, verbose = TRUE) {
> 
>   # ---- reproduce the published matrix + identify the significant set -------
>   long <- ewmv_trait_long(by_block_csv, method)
>   sig <- long %>%
>     filter(!is.na(p_adj), p_adj < alpha) %>%
>     transmute(param, q, cond,
>               prefix = .ROB_COND$prefix[match(cond, .ROB_COND$cond)]) %>%
>     arrange(cond, q, param)
> 
>   if (verbose)
>     cat(sprintf("Significant (Holm p<%.2f) full-sample correlations: %d\n",
>                 alpha, nrow(sig)))
> 
>   d <- utils::read.csv(by_block_csv)
>   if (!"participant_id" %in% names(d) && "sub_id" %in% names(d)) d$participant_id <- d$sub_id
> 
>   # ---- (1) LOO jackknife for every significant cell ------------------------
>   loo_tbl <- pmap_dfr(list(sig$param, sig$q, sig$cond),
>                       ~ .loo_one(d, ..1, ..2, ..3, method = method, alpha = alpha))
> 
>   # ---- (2) posterior propagation -------------------------------------------
>   # Subject-level draws come from the compact per-condition draws file when it
>   # is present (mcmc/ewmv_subject_draws.rds, ~47 MB, shipped with the release);
>   # otherwise they are pulled from the full 3.1 GB combined fits
>   # (mcmc/model_fits_list.rds). Both yield identical subject-ordered draws.
>   if (file.exists(draws_rds)) {
>     if (verbose) cat("Loading compact subject draws for posterior propagation...\n")
>     cdraws <- readRDS(draws_rds)                    # named list keyed by condition
>     fit_for_cond <- function(cond) cdraws[[cond]]
>   } else {
>     if (verbose) cat("Loading full fits for posterior propagation...\n")
>     fits <- readRDS(fits_rds)
>     get_fit <- function(pat) {
>       i <- grep(pat, names(fits), ignore.case = TRUE)
>       if (length(i) != 1) stop("fit pattern '", pat, "' matched ", length(i))
>       fits[[i]]
>     }
>     fit_for_cond <- function(cond) get_fit(.ROB_COND$fit_pat[.ROB_COND$cond == cond])
>   }
>   # cache subject-draw matrices per (cond, param) so we only pull each once
>   needed <- distinct(sig, cond, param)
>   draw_cache <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
>   for (k in seq_len(nrow(needed))) {
>     cd <- needed$cond[k]; pm <- needed$param[k]
>     assign(paste(cd, pm, sep = "||"),
>            .subject_draws(fit_for_cond(cd), pm), envir = draw_cache)
>   }
> 
>   post_tbl <- pmap_dfr(list(sig$param, sig$q, sig$cond), function(pm, qq, cd) {
>     dm <- get(paste(cd, pm, sep = "||"), envir = draw_cache)
>     # fixed trait scores aligned to CSV/draw column order
>     trait <- d[[qq]]
>     stopifnot(length(trait) == ncol(dm))
>     .post_one(dm, trait, pm, qq, cd, method = method)
>   })
> 
>   # ---- combine into one table per correlation ------------------------------
>   tbl <- loo_tbl %>%
>     select(-.loo_r) %>%
>     left_join(post_tbl, by = c("param", "q", "cond")) %>%
>     mutate(
>       param_label = unname(.ECH_PARAMS[param]),
>       q_label     = unname(.ECH_Q[q]),
>       survives    = (!loo_sig_flips) & post_r_excludes_0
>     ) %>%
>     relocate(cond, q_label, param_label) %>%
>     arrange(cond, q_label, param_label)
> 
>   # tuck the raw LOO r vectors alongside for any later drill-down
>   loo_r_vectors <- setNames(loo_tbl$.loo_r,
>                             paste(loo_tbl$cond, loo_tbl$q, loo_tbl$param,
>                                   sep = " | "))
> 
>   summary_txt <- .robustness_summary(tbl)
>   if (verbose) {
>     cat("\n", strrep("=", 70), "\n", sep = "")
>     cat("ROBUSTNESS TABLE (LOO jackknife + posterior propagation)\n")
>     cat(strrep("=", 70), "\n", sep = "")
>     print(.robustness_display(tbl), row.names = FALSE)
>     cat("\n", summary_txt, "\n", sep = "")
>   }
> 
>   invisible(list(table = tbl, long = long, sig = sig,
>                  loo_r_vectors = loo_r_vectors, summary = summary_txt))
> }

text.text: Research using the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) has primarily interpreted behavior as individual differences in risk preference.
However, because participants learn explosion probabilities from experience, performance also reflects latent mechanisms of learning risk contingencies.
We studied these mechanisms using a BART in which learned risk contingencies reversed.
In an online sample of healthy adults (n=118, 63 female), we implemented the BART with three balloon colors of different risk levels.
After 90 trials, color-risk associations of low and high-risk balloons reversed; afterwards participants completed a single-color low-risk control condition.
We fit data from the low-risk balloon, which showed the most behavioral variance, to three candidate hierarchical models separately for each task phase.
We then explored whether schizotypy and psychotic-like experiences were linked to BART performance and model parameters.
Results: Adjusted pumps were not affected by the reversal, nor were they linked with subclinical traits.

The best-performing Exponential Weight Mean Variance (EWMV) model showed a lower inverse temperature (i.e., less systematic responding) after the reversal and a faster shift from prior weighting to accumulated evidence across trials.

In exploratory analyses, higher delusional ideation and positive schizotypy were associated with lower inverse temperature before the reversal; positive and overall schizotypy were associated with greater aversion to outcome variance.
Discussion: Computational modeling revealed latent processes not visible in pumping behavior alone.
Choice stochasticity according to EWMV was higher when multiple contingencies had to be learned and highest after the reversal, though task design limits causal interpretation.
Trait associations were modest and should be interpreted cautiously.

The Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) is one of the most prominent tasks used to investigate risk-taking under uncertainty in psychology research, with reliable correlation to real-world risky behaviors (Lauriola et al., 2014; Lejuez, Aklin, Jones, et al., 2003; Lejuez, Aklin, Zvolensky, et al., 2003; Lejuez et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) is one of the most prominent tasks used to investigate risk-taking under uncertainty in psychology research, with reliable correlation to real-world risky behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lauriola et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lejuez, Aklin, Jones, et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lejuez, Aklin, Zvolensky, et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Lejuez et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, the BART is a computerized task where participants are presented with a series of virtual balloons and decide whether to press a button to pump the balloon, making the balloon grow larger and accumulating a small amount of money in a temporary bank, but also risking the possibility of the balloon exploding and therefore losing all temporary earnings for that trial.
Therefore, before the balloon explodes, participants must decide to end the trial and store their earnings permanently or continue risktaking by pumping the balloon for more money.

In this way risk-taking is expressed through sequential decision making in each trial as reward and risk of explosion increase together over time, and as participants learn the task's uncertain risk contingencies -that is, the underlying levels of explosion risk through trial and error (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: In this way risk-taking is expressed through sequential decision making in each trial as reward and risk of explosion increase together over time, and as participants learn the task's uncertain risk contingencies -that is, the underlying levels of explosion risk through trial and error (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Every balloon in the BART is considered an individual trial, with each trial containing multiple opportunities to pump the balloon.
The standard BART paradigm typically contains 30 trials of a balloon that explodes after an average of 64 pumps, with individual breakpoints drawn from a uniform distribution.
This means explosion occurrence between pumps 1-128 are equally probable before the first pump, whereas the conditional probability of explosion scales higher with each survived pump.

The BART has been used to examine differences in behavior in a variety of contexts such as substance use disorders (Canning et al., 2022) and depression (Blanco et al., 2013), primarily through the statistic of adjusted pumps.
text.formatted: The BART has been used to examine differences in behavior in a variety of contexts such as substance use disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Canning et al., 2022)</ref> and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Blanco et al., 2013)</ref>, primarily through the statistic of adjusted pumps.

text.text: This takes the average pumps for only successfully cashed in balloons across multiple trials and predicts self-reported real-world risky behaviors (Lejuez et al., 2002; Wallsten et al., 2005).
text.formatted: This takes the average pumps for only successfully cashed in balloons across multiple trials and predicts self-reported real-world risky behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lejuez et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wallsten et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: However, the standard BART metric of average adjusted pumps carries two primary limitations.
First, because average adjusted pumps provide a single summary measure of behavior, they cannot distinguish between latent mechanisms that may give rise to the same observed behavior.

These latent mechanisms include how quickly participants learn or update beliefs about riskiness of the balloon, how they weigh prospective gains against potential losses, and how consistently they translate beliefs and valuations into reward-directed action.

If these underlying latent mechanisms are ignored, behavioral differences in the BART cannot confidently be interpreted as altered intentional risk-taking, as two participants who reach the same average through different mechanisms are treated as behaviorally identical.
This limitation has been highlighted in previous BART modeling work (Park et al., 2021; Purcell et al., 2022; Wallsten et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This limitation has been highlighted in previous BART modeling work <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Park et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Purcell et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wallsten et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhou et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The second limitation concerns the selective exclusion of exploded trials (censoring effect): as average adjusted pumps are computed only over balloons that do not explode, it systematically discards every trial pumped to the point of explosion.
This removes high-risk behavior that the BART is designed to elicit and can bias the measure of risk-taking, particularly in participants who experience more explosions (De Groot, 2020).
text.formatted: This removes high-risk behavior that the BART is designed to elicit and can bias the measure of risk-taking, particularly in participants who experience more explosions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(De Groot, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This limitation is especially problematic in BART studies, as participants rarely show adaptive risk-taking strategies in which they learn to pump close to the mean explosion point.
Instead, behavior is often skewed toward lower levels of pumping, which already restricts between-participant variability before the censoring effect reduces it further.
Computational models for the BART address these limitations by modelling each pumping decision directly.

This allows different latent mechanisms underlying task performance such as prior updating, loss aversion, or reward sensitivity, to be identified while using the full trial history, including the trials that end in explosions (Herms et al., 2025; Park et al., 2021; Van Ravenzwaaij et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This allows different latent mechanisms underlying task performance such as prior updating, loss aversion, or reward sensitivity, to be identified while using the full trial history, including the trials that end in explosions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Herms et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Park et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Van Ravenzwaaij et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhou et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Because BART performance demonstrates good test-retest reliability (Li et al., 2020; White et al., 2008), estimating the latent mechanisms alongside average adjusted pumps makes the BART a useful candidate for identifying stable trait-level characteristics of risktaking under uncertainty.
text.formatted: Because BART performance demonstrates good test-retest reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Li et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">White et al., 2008)</ref>, estimating the latent mechanisms alongside average adjusted pumps makes the BART a useful candidate for identifying stable trait-level characteristics of risktaking under uncertainty.

text.text: However, reliability in BART behavioral effects has only been investigated under fixed-contingency conditions and therefore does not speak to whether these latent mechanisms remain stable when risk contingencies change.

Specifically, if individual BART performance reflects a stable tendency toward more risk-averse or riskseeking behavior, relevant model parameters should remain relatively constant across changes in task contingencies.
However, if performance also reflects the capacity to adapt to changing conditions, these parameters should shift when previously learned contingencies no longer apply.

Such a distinction cannot be made with the standard BART task, in which risk contingencies are typically held stable and participants learn a single breakpoint distribution without prior experience of the task.
As a result, it cannot separate participants who adapt slowly overall from those who adapt poorly when conditions change, or indicate how consistent the underlying latent mechanisms are.
This distinction is central to real-world risk taking, where risks and rewards of actions are rarely stationary (Behrens et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This distinction is central to real-world risk taking, where risks and rewards of actions are rarely stationary <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Behrens et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: To accommodate this, we introduce a reversal between multiple learned risk contingencies as a possible methodological extension of the BART.

This creates a scenario where beliefs must be updated against established prior expectations rather than formed from scratch, thereby probing belief updating and risk-taking across two conflicting environments.

As the original BART paper already validated the use of multiple contingencies of varying risk (Lejuez et al., 2002), implementing such a reversal provides a minimal modification of the task while offering a second opportunity to derive parameter estimates that a fixed-contingency task largely constrains during its opening trials.
text.formatted: As the original BART paper already validated the use of multiple contingencies of varying risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lejuez et al., 2002)</ref>, implementing such a reversal provides a minimal modification of the task while offering a second opportunity to derive parameter estimates that a fixed-contingency task largely constrains during its opening trials.

text.text: The combination of BART behavioral decomposition and contingency manipulation should be especially informative in a population for which the summary metric of adjusted pumps is difficult to interpret, and the psychosis spectrum is such a case.

On the BART, people living with schizophrenia consistently show decreased adjusted pumps (Boka et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2012; Msk et al., 2021), despite evidence for increased realworld risky behaviors (Aymerich et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Hunt et al., 2018).
text.formatted: On the BART, people living with schizophrenia consistently show decreased adjusted pumps <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boka et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brown et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cheng et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Msk et al., 2021)</ref>, despite evidence for increased realworld risky behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aymerich et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hunt et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A recent study on psychotic-like experiences has observed a similar trend in the general population (Gabbert et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A recent study on psychotic-like experiences has observed a similar trend in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gabbert et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, interpreting lower adjusted pumps simply as increased riskaversion is too broad, as this interpretation is difficult to reconcile with real-world behavior and remains underexplored across the relevant subclinical continuum.

Decomposition of BART behavior could therefore provide a clearer understanding of whether decreased adjusted pumps reflect altered belief updating about risk, differences in subjective valuation for pumping across a trial, or a more unreliable and stochastic translation of reward expectation into actual behavior (Herms et al., 2025; Purcell et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Decomposition of BART behavior could therefore provide a clearer understanding of whether decreased adjusted pumps reflect altered belief updating about risk, differences in subjective valuation for pumping across a trial, or a more unreliable and stochastic translation of reward expectation into actual behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Herms et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Purcell et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The reversal of risk contingencies further strengthens the case for a trait-level investigation, as reversal learning studies indicate alterations in cognitive flexibility and reward-learning in the psychosis spectrum (Baker et al., 2023; Kesby et al., 2023; Koch et al., 2010; Schlagenhauf et al., 2014; Waltz, 2017).
text.formatted: The reversal of risk contingencies further strengthens the case for a trait-level investigation, as reversal learning studies indicate alterations in cognitive flexibility and reward-learning in the psychosis spectrum <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baker et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kesby et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Koch et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schlagenhauf et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Waltz, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This provides an informed target for detecting differences in adaptive updating that may be missed by fixed-contingency tasks.

Further, these latent mechanisms may relate differentially to traits analogous to positive (e.g. hallucinations and delusions) and negative (e.g. blunted affect and amotivation) symptom domains, providing a testable framework for describing individual differences in risk-taking in the general population (Fervaha et al., 2014; Purcell et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Further, these latent mechanisms may relate differentially to traits analogous to positive (e.g. hallucinations and delusions) and negative (e.g. blunted affect and amotivation) symptom domains, providing a testable framework for describing individual differences in risk-taking in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fervaha et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Purcell et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The primary objective of the present study was to investigate whether computational decomposition of BART behavior, combined with a manipulation of already learned risk contingencies, could identify individual differences in risk-taking that are not captured by adjusted pumps alone in fixed-contingency task variants.

To test this, we assessed schizotypal traits alongside subclinical psychotic-like experiences and examined whether a reversal of learned contingencies could clarify how latent BART mechanisms relate to specific trait domains.

Importantly, this allowed us to compare which associations between traits and risktaking are implicated when learning contingencies from a naïve starting point versus when prior contingencies had already established associations resulting in participants' personal risk-taking behavior.

Based on previous findings on the BART and reversal learning in schizophrenia, we hypothesized that higher levels of schizotypal traits would be associated with a lower number of adjusted pumps and slower adaptive belief updating following the contingency reversal.
This directional hypothesis is largely motivated by previous work examining performance on the BART in psychosis (Purcell et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This directional hypothesis is largely motivated by previous work examining performance on the BART in psychosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Purcell et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, broader computational findings do not indicate a uniform directional impairment in belief updating.

Evidence suggests context-dependent abnormalities in precision weighting, including heightened volatility estimates and increased switching, suggesting that excessive or insufficient updating may depend on symptom domain and task (Fromm et al., 2022; Katthagen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Evidence suggests context-dependent abnormalities in precision weighting, including heightened volatility estimates and increased switching, suggesting that excessive or insufficient updating may depend on symptom domain and task <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fromm et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Katthagen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Aside from this, because the candidate models presented in the Methods assume distinct and not directly comparable latent constructs, we did not specify directional hypotheses for individual model parameters; and parameter-level trait associations were therefore treated as exploratory following model comparison.

Our analysis included 118 participants (mean age: 41.3, range: 18-68; 63 female, 52 male, 3 diverse) from the online platform Prolific who had an approval rating of at least 95% on Prolific and at least 20 studies completed previously.

We originally recruited 175 participants from Prolific, but 57 were excluded due to technical issues (2), withdrawn consent (3), or failed attention checks (52) which were placed within the subclinical and demographic questionnaires.
Base compensation of at least £6 per hour was given to each participant, with bonus earnings based on BART performance.

After all questionnaires and tasks were completed, participants also completed the Berlin Estimate Adjustment Task (Molleman et al., 2019), a social information use task which is not the focus of this study.

text.text: In the first set of 90 trials pre-reversal, breakpoints were as follows: blue (average breakpoint: 64, max possible: 128), yellow (average breakpoint: 16, max possible: 32), and orange (average breakpoint: 4, max possible: 8); the first 30 balloons presented a randomized mixture of the different balloon colors (10 of each color), followed by 20 trials for each color individually.
After this, a reversal occurred between the breakpoint distributions of the blue balloon and orange balloon, switching the high-risk balloon and low-risk balloons risk-color mappings.
Then, the same paradigm was repeated for another 90 trials.

Participants were rewarded with bonus earnings of 0.3 pence (GBP) per pump for successfully cashed-in trials due to the large amount of trials presented, and this was determined to provide a meaningful monetary incentive according to average scores from university students testing our technical implementation of the task.

A virtual piggy bank displayed the increasing earnings with each pump, resetting back to the value of the previous trial upon explosion and updating the total earnings for the next trial upon successful cash-in.

The reversal of risk contingencies between low-risk and high-risk balloons allowed us to evaluate changes in participant behavior when the previously punishing orange balloon became the balloon with the most opportunity for reward in the task.

This also allowed us to compare parameter values between task phases, noting that models were fit separately and therefore did not explicitly instantiate color-specific latent beliefs across the reversal.

Participants were not informed of risk probabilities of the balloons or the existence of risk-level differences between colors, and they subsequently had to discover the average breakpoints through trial and error to maximize earnings.

All participants received the same order of balloon colors and break points according to Lejuez (2002), which increased reliability of observing individual differences in risky behavior at the expense of generalizability of findings.

text.text: We expected to see slower learning in the orange post-reversal blocks than the blue pre-reversal blocks, since the orange balloon was previously associated with a more punishing explosion probability.

To accommodate the censoring effect, where exclusion of exploded trials in adjusted pumps biases risk-taking behavior, we also ran post hoc tests across blocks including average pumps for all trials in a block without excluding exploded trials.

We then tested whether subclinical psychosis-spectrum scores predicted BART behavior using linear regression, fitting separate models for each score (CAPS, PDI, SPQ) predicting average adjusted pumps and average explosions within each condition for the low-risk balloon.

text.text: To find the most suitable model parameters for our data we compared model performance using leave-one-out cross-validation information criterion (LOOIC) to evaluate predictive accuracy while penalizing model complexity.

As parameters for the models are only interpretable if they can be recovered from the data, we first performed parameter recovery for the winning model to determine model consistency across the separately fit conditions by drawing parameters from each condition's fitted population (group mean ±SD), simulating
BART data from the model on that condition's real breakpoints, refitting the model, and then correlating true vs. recovered per-participant values.
We then used Bayesian group-level parameter contrasts to assess overall differences in parameter values across the entire sample between the pre-reversal, post-reversal, and control conditions.
Pearson correlations were used to examine the relationship between subclinical measures and model parameters across conditions.
Given the available sample sizes of n=117-118, estimated power ranged from approximately 0.55 to 0.85 for detecting correlations of approximately r=0.22-0.31.

This was followed by Steiger-Williams tests to investigate significance of correlations before and after the reversal, and we re-ran the correlation analyses leaving each participant out to see the effect of the most influential participants on the correlations.

Finally, for holm-significant trait-parameter associations we also entered standardized questionnaire scores as participant-level predictors of the corresponding EWMV parameters in separate hierarchical refits (1,000 warmup, 2000 samples), allowing trait effects to be estimated while propagating uncertainty in individual estimates.
Adjusted pumps and earnings were higher for balloons with higher predefined breakpoints, while explosions were less frequent in these balloons.

text.text: Because reward per pump differed between tasks, we also expressed earnings as a percentage of the maximum possible earnings in each task.

Performance relative to the maximum did not differ significantly between the reversal task (M=19.65%, SD=6.70%) and the control task (M=20.59%, SD=8.05%; paired t-test, t(117)=-1.63, p=0.105, 95% CI [-2.07, 0.20]).

Consistent with previous BART behavioral findings, adjusted pumps were not normally distributed but right-skewed, indicating that participants rarely adopt an adaptive risk-taking strategy of pumping close to the average breakpoint, even when such a strategy would have increased potential earnings.

While this may be due in part to chance variation in participant behavior, this pattern is consistent with the censoring effect described by De Groot (2020) whereby excluding exploded trials can bias the pump metric downward and reduce observable variance in risktaking across the sample.
Separate regressions of subclinical scores on average adjusted pumps and explosions showed no significant association in any condition.

As an additional manipulation check, high-risk adjusted pumps differed slightly between pre-reversal orange and post-reversal blue balloons (t(68)=-2.10, p=0.039, 95% CI [-0.34, -0.01]), with a significant phase x block interaction (F(1.72,152.65)=6.12, p=0.004, η²G=0.014).

Pre-reversal, participants were entirely naïve to balloon contingencies (e.g., blue: most rewarding), whereas the post-reversal, the most punishing balloon color became the most rewarding (i.e. orange), and the control balloon (i.e. pink) was tested in a separate set of single fixed-contingency trials.

text.text: After the reversal, the most pronounced change in parameter values was observed for inverse temperature: participants translated learned value into pumping less reliably and consequently exhibited more stochastic behavior than pre-reversal (Δ=-1.11, 95% CrI [-1.82, -0.42]).
Behavior was most consistent in the control condition, higher than both pre-reversal (Δ=1.28, 95% CrI [0.45, 2.11]) and post-reversal (Δ=2.39, 95% CrI [1.61, 3.18]).
Together, these contrasts demonstrated that decision noise, and the resulting reduction in behavioral consistency increased with the competing demands imposed by the task.

Behavior was most consistent under a single contingency, less consistency with multiple contingencies, and least consistent when multiple contingencies were presented after beliefs had been violated by the reversal.

Participants did not show credible differences in the prior weight after the reversal compared to before, suggesting that initial expectations were not markedly more optimistic or pessimistic following the change in contingencies (prior weight: -0.003, [-0.013, 0.008]).
In the control condition, however, participants showed more optimistic prior expectations than pre-reversal (prior weight: Δ = -0.011, 95% CrI [-0.016, -0.006]).
The contrast control and post-reversal conditions pointed in the same direction but spanned zero (prior weight: Δ=-0.008, 95% CrI [-0.018, 0.001]).
Belief updating differed more clearly between conditions.

The EWMV updating exponent was higher post-reversal than pre-reversal, indicating a faster model-implied shift from prior weighting toward accumulated evidence (updating exponent: Δ=0.004, 95% CrI [0.0008, 0.007]).
The updating exponent was lower in the control condition than in both the pre-reversal (Δ=-0.002, 95% CrI [-0.0038, -0.0001]) and post-reversal phases (Δ=-0.006, 95% CrI [-0.009, -0.003]).
When estimating the subjective value of making an additional pump on a trial, explosions were weighed less heavily after the reversal than before (loss aversion: Δ=-1.03, 95% CrI [-1.99, -0.05]).

However, the control condition did not differ credibly from postreversal (loss aversion: Δ=0.33, 95% CrI [-0.54, 1.17]), and the difference between the control and the pre-reversal condition also spanned zero (loss aversion: Δ=-0.70, 95% CrI [-1.55, 0.11]).
Therefore, the reduction in post-reversal loss aversion is not interpreted as reversal specific.

In this study, we implemented a modified version of the BART containing multiple risk contingencies (Lejuez et al., 2002) and introduced a reversal between high-risk and low-risk balloons.
text.formatted: In this study, we implemented a modified version of the BART containing multiple risk contingencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lejuez et al., 2002)</ref> and introduced a reversal between high-risk and low-risk balloons.

text.text: This allowed us to test whether behavioral and computational differences emerge when participants must update previously learned risk contingencies rather than learn from a naïve starting point.
Behaviorally, adjusted pumps did not differ reliably between pre-and postreversal conditions, and subclinical psychosis-spectrum traits were not associated with adjusted pumps or explosions.

However, when all trials were included rather than only successfully cashed-in trials, condition differences emerged in the middle low-risk balloon block, consistent with the censoring problem described for adjusted pumps in the BART (De Groot, 2020).
Computationally, the EWMV model provided the best fit across conditions and showed reliable recovery for most parameters, except risk preference.

Parameter contrasts suggested that behavior became less consistent after the reversal, with lower inverse temperature indicating more stochastic pumping, alongside faster belief updating and reduced loss aversion post-reversal.
Trait-parameter associations were modest, providing limited evidence linking subclinical psychosis-spectrum traits to how computational mechanisms of BART performance changed across task phases.
The central methodological contribution of this study is the introduction of a within-task contingency reversal to the BART (Lauriola et al., 2014; Lejuez et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The central methodological contribution of this study is the introduction of a within-task contingency reversal to the BART <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lauriola et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Lejuez et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Standard BART implementations are useful for assessing risk-taking under uncertainty, but they typically hold risk contingencies stable and therefore primarily capture learning from a naïve starting point.
Real-world risk-taking, however, often occurs in changing environments, where previously learned contingencies may no longer apply.
Adaptive behavior then requires individuals to detect change, update beliefs about the probability of negative outcomes, and adjust behavior accordingly (Behrens et al., 2007; Findling et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Adaptive behavior then requires individuals to detect change, update beliefs about the probability of negative outcomes, and adjust behavior accordingly <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Findling et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is central to theories of learning under volatility, which propose that learning rates should increase when environments become unstable or when recent outcomes indicate that previous beliefs are no longer reliable (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010 Nassar et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: This distinction is central to theories of learning under volatility, which propose that learning rates should increase when environments become unstable or when recent outcomes indicate that previous beliefs are no longer reliable <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Nassar et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Nassar et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: The present manipulation therefore extends the BART from a task of risk-taking under stable uncertainty to one that also probes adaptation to a change in risk contingencies.

This extension links the BART more directly to reversal-learning paradigms, which are widely used to assess cognitive flexibility and the updating of stimulus-outcome associations after changes in reinforcement contingencies (Izquierdo et al., 2017; Kesby et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This extension links the BART more directly to reversal-learning paradigms, which are widely used to assess cognitive flexibility and the updating of stimulus-outcome associations after changes in reinforcement contingencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Izquierdo et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kesby et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Reversal learning has been especially informative in psychiatric research such as psychosis because it separates initial acquisition of reward associations from the ability to revise those associations when contingencies change.

Individuals with schizophrenia show impairments in probabilistic reversal learning, often linked to orbitofrontal, frontostriatal, and cognitive-control dysfunction (Reddy et al., 2016; Waltz & Gold, 2007).
text.formatted: Individuals with schizophrenia show impairments in probabilistic reversal learning, often linked to orbitofrontal, frontostriatal, and cognitive-control dysfunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Reddy et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Waltz & Gold, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroimaging further suggests altered ventral striatal prediction-error signaling and altered recruitment of control regions during feedback-driven updating in schizophrenia (Culbreth et al., 2016; Schlagenhauf et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Neuroimaging further suggests altered ventral striatal prediction-error signaling and altered recruitment of control regions during feedback-driven updating in schizophrenia <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Culbreth et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schlagenhauf et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: More recent work emphasizes that reversal-learning impairments may reflect heterogeneous mechanisms, including altered loss sensitivity, impaired goal-directed control, or inconsistent use of learned reward information (Baker et al., 2023; MacDonald III et al., 2025; Suetani et al., 2022).
text.formatted: More recent work emphasizes that reversal-learning impairments may reflect heterogeneous mechanisms, including altered loss sensitivity, impaired goal-directed control, or inconsistent use of learned reward information <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baker et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">MacDonald III et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Suetani et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The current BART reversal builds on this literature by embedding adaptive updating within a risk-taking task involving accumulating gains, potential losses, and repeated decisions to continue or stop.
The absence of robust pre-to post-reversal differences in adjusted pumps should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the reversal had no effect.
Adjusted pumps exclude trials on which participants pump to the point of explosion, thereby removing trials that may contain the strongest information about high-risk behavior.

This censoring problem has been highlighted in methodological work on the BART, as exploded trials may reveal the level of risk participants were willing to take but are omitted from the standard adjusted-pumps metric (Coon & Lee, 2022; De Groot, 2020; Young & McCoy, 2019).
text.formatted: This censoring problem has been highlighted in methodological work on the BART, as exploded trials may reveal the level of risk participants were willing to take but are omitted from the standard adjusted-pumps metric <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Coon & Lee, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">De Groot, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Young & McCoy, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Our finding that condition differences emerged when all trials were included, but not when using adjusted pumps, supports this concern and suggests that standard behavioral summaries may obscure condition effects when exploded trials carry meaningful information.
Computational modelling results further support the value of decomposing BART performance beyond adjusted pumps.

The EWMV model provided the best fit across all conditions, extending previous work showing that BART behavior is well captured by a model combining exponentially weighted belief updating with subjective valuation of gains, losses, and outcome variance (Park et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The EWMV model provided the best fit across all conditions, extending previous work showing that BART behavior is well captured by a model combining exponentially weighted belief updating with subjective valuation of gains, losses, and outcome variance <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Park et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, this model performed well in the control condition, which most closely resembles a fixed-contingency task, but also in the reversal condition, where participants had to update previously learned associations.
Although model diagnostics were satisfactory for risk preference, it was the parameter with the weakest recovery, replicating concerns raised by Park et al. (2021).
text.formatted: Although model diagnostics were satisfactory for risk preference, it was the parameter with the weakest recovery, replicating concerns raised by <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Park et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore interpret its trait associations as suggestive rather than robust.
Model adequacy was additionally assessed using history-conditioned and fully generative posterior predictive checks (Supplementary Figure 2a-b).
text.formatted: Model adequacy was additionally assessed using history-conditioned and fully generative posterior predictive checks (Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a-b</ref>).

text.text: The most robust task phase effect was observed for inverse temperature, which reflects choice consistency relative to the EWMV subjective value estimation.
Parameter contrasts demonstrated the highest group-level consistency in the control condition, less consistency in the pre-reversal condition, and the least consistency after the reversal.
One explanation for this is that the reversal did not simply change how much risk participants took but reduced the consistency with which a learned value was translated into pumping behavior.

This is important because reversal learning is often discussed in terms of whether participants update beliefs, but adaptive behavior also requires that updated beliefs guide action (Behrens et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This is important because reversal learning is often discussed in terms of whether participants update beliefs, but adaptive behavior also requires that updated beliefs guide action <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Behrens et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In the present task, the reversal may therefore have increased decision noise or reduced exploitation of learned value rather than producing a simple failure to update.

However, lower inverse temperature cannot be interpreted as uniquely reflecting increased decision noise due to task complexity, because of the confounding factors such as the difference in monetary incentives between the reversal and control tasks and the separate model fits for each task phase.

The updating exponent indicated that the fastest group-level shift from prior weighting to accumulated evidence occurred in the post-reversal phase, whereas the slowest shift occurred in the control condition.

This may partly reflect the influence of outcomes encountered at early balloons, but it may also indicate that surprising outcomes carry greater informational weight when they violate an established expectation, consistent with models of prediction error updating and adaptive learning under volatility (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010 Nassar et al., , 2012;; Soltani & Izquierdo, 2019).
text.formatted: This may partly reflect the influence of outcomes encountered at early balloons, but it may also indicate that surprising outcomes carry greater informational weight when they violate an established expectation, consistent with models of prediction error updating and adaptive learning under volatility <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Nassar et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Nassar et al., , 2012;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Soltani & Izquierdo, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, our design contained a single contingency reversal and did not manipulate environmental volatility.

In addition, the EWMV updating exponent is estimated separately within each task phase, so it provides neither a trial-varying learning rate nor a direct estimate of a participant's perception of environmental volatility.

The present results therefore show a faster shift from prior weighting toward accumulated evidence after a contingency change, but they cannot show whether this shift reflects volatility-sensitive learning.
Testing this would require task designs with multiple contingency changes and models that estimate adaptive updating in a changing environment.
At the behavioral level, CAPS, PDI, and SPQ scores were not associated with adjusted pumps or explosions.
This null finding is informative considering the mixed literature on BART performance in psychosis.

Some studies report reduced adjusted pumps or more conservative BART behavior in schizophrenia, often interpreted as increased risk aversion or altered riskreward learning (Cheng et al., 2012; Gabbert et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Some studies report reduced adjusted pumps or more conservative BART behavior in schizophrenia, often interpreted as increased risk aversion or altered riskreward learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cheng et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gabbert et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, this interpretation is not straightforward, as reduced pumping in the BART does not necessarily map onto lower realworld risk-taking.
Recent work suggests that BART effects may be small, symptom-dependent, or detectable only in larger samples.

For example, Patel et al. (2025) found that avolition predicted variability in optimal risk-taking in early psychosis, whereas Gabbert et al. (2024) reported BART-related differences in relation to psychotic-like experiences in a larger generalpopulation sample.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Patel et al. (2025)</ref> found that avolition predicted variability in optimal risk-taking in early psychosis, whereas <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gabbert et al. (2024)</ref> reported BART-related differences in relation to psychotic-like experiences in a larger generalpopulation sample.

text.text: Thus, the absence of behavioral trait associations in the current study may reflect limited power and restricted subclinical symptom variability, but it also reinforces the broader point that adjusted pumps may be too coarse to capture mechanisms linking psychosis-spectrum traits to risk-taking.
The combination of computational decomposition and contingency manipulation may therefore be especially useful for psychosis-spectrum research (R. A. Adams et al., 2013; Mombelli et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The combination of computational decomposition and contingency manipulation may therefore be especially useful for psychosis-spectrum research (R. A. <ref type="bibr">Adams et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Mombelli et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Lower adjusted pumps could arise from more pessimistic prior expectations, faster updating after negative outcomes, stronger loss aversion, lower reward sensitivity, greater sensitivity to outcome variance, or less consistent translation of value into action.

These mechanisms have different theoretical implications but can produce similar behavioral averages, a problem emphasized in recent work on risky decision-making and computational psychiatry (Purcell et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These mechanisms have different theoretical implications but can produce similar behavioral averages, a problem emphasized in recent work on risky decision-making and computational psychiatry <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Purcell et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: By comparing naïve learning, belief-informed reversal learning, and a fixed-contingency control condition, the present paradigm provides a way to ask whether psychosis-spectrum traits are associated with initial risk learning, adaptive updating after contingency change, subjective valuation of potential losses, or consistency of value-guided action.
In the exploratory analyses, the clearest link was between higher positive schizotypy and delusional ideation and lower inverse temperature in the pre-reversal and control conditions.

This association is conceptually meaningful, as lower inverse temperature does not directly imply impaired learning of balloon contingencies, but instead less consistent translation of the model's subjective value estimates into behavior.
However, inverse temperature is not specific to a single cognitive mechanism.

Greater EWMV-estimated behavioral stochasticity may reflect several processes, including inefficient reward exploitation (MacDonald III et al., 2025), strategy switching or altered inferences under uncertainty (Fromm et al., 2022; Katthagen et al., 2022), or variation from more automatic response processes not represented by the EWMV (Zhou & Pitt, 2024).

text.text: Lower inverse temperature and its association with positive schizotypy and delusional ideation should therefore be interpreted as greater model-estimated behavioral stochasticity, not as pointing to a specific latent mechanism.

Because these associations appeared only in conditions with naïve expectations, as opposed to the postreversal condition where expectations for color-risk associations had already been informed by experience, these associations may reflect individual differences in initial task learning that diminish once contingencies are acquired.
However, the pre-and post-reversal correlations did not differ significantly (Steiger-Williams tests, Supplementary Table 10).
text.formatted: However, the pre-and post-reversal correlations did not differ significantly (Steiger-Williams tests, Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">10</ref>).

text.text: The reversal manipulation may therefore be valuable in future studies of clinically relevant groups.
In schizophrenia, first-episode psychosis, or clinical high-risk samples, a reversedcontingency BART could test whether different symptom dimensions map onto distinct computational profiles.

Positive symptoms may relate more closely to altered prior beliefs, aberrant belief updating, or heightened sensitivity to surprising outcomes, consistent with computational accounts of psychosis emphasizing abnormal inference, aberrant salience, and altered weighting of priors and prediction errors (R. Adams et al., 2013; Goodwin et al., 2026; Kapur, 2003; Sterzer et al., 2018).

text.text: Negative symptoms, by contrast, may relate more closely to reduced precision of value-guided action, reduced motivation to exploit learned reward opportunities, or greater inconsistency in translating subjective value into behavior (Gold et al., 2012; Millman et al., 2026; Murray et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Negative symptoms, by contrast, may relate more closely to reduced precision of value-guided action, reduced motivation to exploit learned reward opportunities, or greater inconsistency in translating subjective value into behavior <ref type="bibr">(Gold et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Millman et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Murray et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: A reversal design is well suited to testing this distinction because it asks not only how participants learn risk contingencies, but also whether they can flexibly revise and use those contingencies when the environment changes.

Together, these findings suggest that a reversed-contingency BART can provide a useful framework for studying adaptive risk-taking, although several methodological considerations should be addressed in future work.

First, the study was conducted online in a non-clinical sample with subclinical variation in psychosis-spectrum traits, limiting conclusions about clinical psychosis and possibly reducing power to detect reliable trait associations.

Excluding 52 of 175 participants (29.7%) for failing attention checks further reduced statistical power and may limit the generalizability of the trait findings, although the full and retained samples did not differ significantly on any behavioral or questionnaire measures, with full comparisons listed in the supplementary materials (Table 12).

text.text: Second, our initial training of the BART only showed ten possible pumps before explosions, and though this was communicated as an example and that the balloon may grow larger, it likely set a precedent for why average adjusted pumps is lower in our sample than Lejuez et al. (2002).

(2002)</ref>.

text.text: With this, the previously mentioned difference in monetary incentives between the reversal and control tasks may contribute to behavioral differences as well.
However, prior work on the BART suggests that larger real monetary rewards may reduce pumping behavior rather than increase it (Xu et al., 2013).
text.formatted: However, prior work on the BART suggests that larger real monetary rewards may reduce pumping behavior rather than increase it <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Xu et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Regardless, because incentive magnitude differed between tasks, differences in pumping behavior and model estimates for choice consistency cannot be uniquely attributed to task complexity.

Third, the task design involves several confounds: task phase was confounded with balloon color, serial position within the task, and accumulated task experience, while the control condition was always after the reversal task.
Although a reversal necessarily changes the relationship between stimulus identity and contingency within a participant, the fixed colorrisk mappings were not counterbalanced across participants.
Similarly, we did not counterbalance task order between reversal and control conditions, which future studies should consider if implementing two versions of the BART.

It is also possible that differences in recruitment could induce part of the differences seen between reversal and control blocks due to individuals who completed all tasks at once experiencing more fatigue, though performance between recruitments on the control BART did not significantly differ (see Supplementary Table 3).

text.text: All individuals also received the same order of trials in terms of balloon color and breakpoint, and though this is typical within the BART to maximize individual differences in risk-taking behavior (Lejuez et al., 2002), it restricts the generalizability of findings.

text.text: Although balloon order was randomized within the pre-and post-reversal blocks when generating this sequence, color-contingency sequences were not counterbalanced or fully matched before and after reversal.
Fourth, the computational models were fitted only to the low-risk balloon and separately within each task phase.
This limits how well the models can represent interactions across contingencies or continuous latent beliefs across the reversal.
We chose this approach because the STL scales its estimates by the design parameter nmax, the upper bound of the breakpoint distribution, even though participants do not know this value.

Extending the STL across contingencies with different breakpoint distributions would therefore require a substantially larger modification than extending the 4PAR or EWMV to track participants' target pump numbers across the reversal.
In addition, we did not perform a formal model recovery analysis, so the model comparison does not establish that the three models can be reliably distinguished when the generating model is known.
Fifth, risk preference in the EWMV model recovered weakly and showed compression toward the group mean, consistent with previous observations for this model (Park et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Fifth, risk preference in the EWMV model recovered weakly and showed compression toward the group mean, consistent with previous observations for this model <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Park et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the trait analyses were exploratory and involved multiple parameter-trait associations, which require replication in larger samples.
Overall, the present findings suggest that adding a contingency reversal to the BART provides a useful methodological extension for studying risk-taking under changing environmental demands.

The manipulation revealed computational differences that were not captured by adjusted pumps alone and thus highlighted the importance of modelling full trial history rather than relying exclusively on successful cash-out trials.

The strongest reversalrelated effect was reduced choice consistency after contingency change, suggesting that adaptation may be expressed not only in what participants learn but also in how reliably learned value is translated into action.
Associations with subclinical psychosis-spectrum traits were modest, providing limited evidence for robust trait-level effects in the present sample.

Nevertheless, the approach offers a promising framework for future clinical studies aiming to separate risk learning, belief updating, valuation, and action consistency in psychosisspectrum populations.
